concepts.title: Habits
concepts.hook: Missing one day did not undo a new habit in Lally's study. Habits took anywhere from 18 to 254 days to settle in.
concepts.rule: A cue can start a learned act. Repeating it in the same place makes the link stronger. In Lally's study, habits took very different times to settle, and one missed day did not undo them.

claims.text: Cues in a stable setting can bring back a learned action.
In Lally and team’s study, modeled times ranged from 18 to 254 days; one missed chance did not undo habit growth.
In that study, the typical time to near full habit strength was 66 days.

items.stem: Every night after hostel dinner, Nikhil sits at the same desk and picks up his notebook. What sets this off?

options.feedback: The repeated setting can bring back the learned act before he thinks much about a goal.

options.text: Hitting a fixed number of practice days.
options.feedback: Repeating matters, so a fixed day count sounds useful. But here the familiar desk is the cue that starts the action.
Willpower can start an act, but here the same dinner and desk come first each day. That steady setting is the cue.

items.stem: Tara sketches every evening, but skips one day in exam week. What happens to the habit?

options.feedback: In the study, missing a day now and then did not wipe out the habit built so far.
One gap can feel like a reset. The learned cue link can still be there the next day.

options.text: She must start a 21-day count again.
options.feedback: Lally's study found no fixed day count, and one miss did not undo earlier habit growth.

items.stem: People say a habit takes 21 days. In a real study, about how many days did a typical habit take to feel automatic?

options.feedback: The middle person in the study took 66 days. Others took anywhere from 18 to 254 days.
The 21-day rule is easy to remember. In the study, the middle person took 66 days, and the spread was wide.
That was the slowest person in the study, not the middle one. The middle person took 66 days.

items.stem: Riya hangs her bag on a hook, then opens a music app. She does this every day. What starts the app habit?

options.text: Hanging the bag on the hook.
options.feedback: The repeated place can become linked to the act even when the student's goal changes.
A goal can motivate app use, but the bag on the hook is the immediate cue that precedes this repeated action.
That music comes after the act, so it cannot start it. The bag on the hook comes first.

items.stem: Arjun moves to a new room. He still wants to practise, but he does it less. Why?

options.text: The old room's cue is gone.
options.feedback: The repeated setting can trigger the action; a new room may not provide that learned cue.

options.text: A strong goal works in any room.
options.feedback: The goal stays the same, so this feels right. The old cue may be gone.

options.text: The goal alone brings back the old cue.
options.feedback: The goal is still there, but it does not bring back the old room cue on its own.

items.stem: A cue is something around you that starts a habit. It is part of the ___.

options.feedback: A habit links an action to the things around it, such as the place you are in or what you just did.
A reward can follow an act, so it is easy to mix up. A cue comes first.
A written goal can help, but a cue is a feature of the setting just before the act, like a place.

items.stem: Kabir built a habit in 21 days. His coach says the whole team will too. What is wrong with that?

options.text: Each person and habit takes its own time.
options.feedback: One person's timing cannot set a deadline for everyone. In the study, people took very different numbers of weeks.
One clear number is easy to teach. The study found wide gaps across acts and people.

options.text: Using the same cue makes everyone match by day 21.
options.feedback: A shared cue need not make different people reach the same habit strength on one day.

items.stem: Put Ravi's phone habit in order.

options.text: Ravi gets home and drops his bag on the bed.
options.feedback: This usual moment is the cue. It comes first and sets the loop going.

options.text: He picks up his phone without much thought.
options.feedback: After many repeats, the cue can start the learned act with little thought.

options.text: A new message gives a small lift, and the link grows.
options.feedback: A pay-off after the act can make the cue and act more tightly linked over time.

misconceptions.name: One fixed day count
misconceptions.correction: Habit time varies by person and act; there is no fixed day count.

misconceptions.name: One miss resets all
misconceptions.correction: One missed chance did not wipe out habit growth in the study.

misconceptions.name: Goal replaces cue
misconceptions.correction: A steady goal may not start a habit when a usual cue is gone.

quest.title: Spot a cue
quest.detail: Watch one harmless daily act. Name the cue, the act, and the good result that may help it recur.

steps.title: A cue starts a habit

hook.stem: Why do many people grab their phone the moment they get home?

options.feedback: Right. Something just before the act can start it. That is a cue.

options.text: They decide to, every single time.
options.feedback: Often there is no fresh decision. Something just before the act sets it off.

options.text: Phones send more alerts in the evening.
options.feedback: Alerts can pull us in, but the grab happens even with no alert.

steps.teach: A habit often starts with a cue: a place, a time or an act just before it. The cue sets the habit off with little thought.

parts: After brushing his teeth,
Arun does ten push-ups.
example.spot: After brushing his teeth,
example.feedback: Brushing his teeth comes just before the push-ups, so it is the cue.

guided.stem: Every time Meera sits on the bus, she opens a game. What is the cue?
guided.hint: The cue comes just before the act.

options.feedback: Yes. Sitting down comes first and sets the game off.
Opening the game is the act itself. The cue comes just before it.
Winning comes after the act, so it is the reward, not the cue.

guided.stem: Ravi studies well at the library desk, but not at home. What might be missing at home?
guided.hint: Which thing is only in one place?

options.feedback: Right. The library desk is the cue, and home does not have it.
His goal goes with him. What stays behind is the cue of the desk.
He can carry books home. The library desk itself is the cue he leaves behind.

steps.takeaway: Find the cue, and you find what starts the habit.

steps.title: Repeats in one setting make it stronger

hook.stem: You always study in one corner of your room. What happens when you sit there?

options.feedback: Yes. Doing it again and again in one spot ties the spot to the act.
Places do matter. A spot you repeat an act in can start that act.
Repeats in one spot usually make the act easier to start, not harder.

steps.teach: Each time you repeat an act in the same setting, the link between cue and act gets stronger. A new setting can weaken it.

parts: For a month, Sana walks
at the same park gate
each morning, and now her feet head there by themselves.
example.spot: at the same park gate
example.feedback: The same gate every morning is the stable setting that made the link strong.

guided.stem: Dev revises at the same desk every evening. Now sitting there makes him reach for his notes. Why?
guided.hint: What has he done again and again in one place?

options.feedback: Right. Repeating the act at one desk made the desk a strong cue.
Comfort helps a little, but the repeats in one place built the link.

options.text: He made a new decision tonight.
options.feedback: No fresh decision is needed. The repeated setting does the work.

guided.stem: Asha always skips rope in her yard. On a trip, she forgets to skip at all. Why?
guided.hint: What is missing on the trip?

options.text: Her yard cue is not there.
options.feedback: Yes. Away from the yard, the cue that set off her habit is gone.
Her liking did not change. The setting that cued it did.
Habits do not expire. A new place just removes the usual cue.

steps.takeaway: Same place, same act, again and again: the link grows.

steps.title: It takes weeks, and one miss is fine

hook.stem: A poster says every habit takes exactly 21 days. Is that right?

options.feedback: Right. In one study it took from 18 to 254 days.
The 21-day rule is a myth. In one study the time ranged from 18 to 254 days.
Most habits took much longer. The typical one took about two months.

steps.teach: A new habit takes weeks, and the time varies a lot from person to person. Missing one day does not wipe it out.

visual.label: Days until a habit felt automatic, in one study

example.ask: Tap what happened after the miss.
parts: Meena missed her morning run once.
The next day, the run still felt automatic.
example.spot: The next day, the run still felt automatic.
example.feedback: One missed day did not reset her habit. It was still there the next day.

guided.stem: Kiran has meditated daily for three weeks, but it still takes effort. What does this show?
guided.hint: In one study the typical habit took about two months.

options.text: Habits often take longer than three weeks.
options.feedback: Yes. Three weeks is early. Many habits need about two months or more.
Not at all. Taking longer than 21 days is normal.
It can still form. Many habits take two months or more.

guided.stem: Pooja skips her evening reading once during a wedding. What happens next?
guided.hint: Does one gap wipe out weeks of repeats?

options.feedback: Right. One missed day did not undo habit growth in the study.
One miss does not reset a habit to zero.
There is no 21-day wait. She can just carry on the next day.

steps.takeaway: Give it weeks, and do not worry about one missed day.

concepts.title: Loss aversion
concepts.hook: In choice studies, losing ₹100 often feels worse than winning ₹100 feels good.
concepts.rule: Loss aversion is a pattern where a loss can feel stronger than a same-size gain. It is a tendency in choices, not a law for every person or every case.

claims.text: Prospect theory treats gains and losses relative to a reference point.
Losses can weigh more than equal gains in choice.

items.stem: At a hostel game, Dev has ten tokens. Which feels bigger: losing one, or winning one?

options.feedback: Gains and losses are felt from a starting point, and a loss often weighs more than a gain of the same size.
The token amounts match, so equal feelings seem fair. A loss may feel stronger.
It is the other way round. A loss usually weighs more than a gain of the same size.

items.stem: Meera is given ₹50. She can bet it to win ₹50 more, or lose it. What pulls hardest on her choice?

options.text: Fear of losing the ₹50 she has.
options.feedback: Once the amount feels owned, giving it up can weigh more than a same-size gain.

options.text: Only the chance to win more.
options.feedback: The extra ₹50 draws the eye. Losing the ₹50 already held can also shape the choice.
Small sums can still pull on a choice. Losing the ₹50 already held often weighs more than gaining ₹50.

items.stem: Say a 10-point loss hurts twice as much as a 10-point gain feels good. How many points must you gain to balance the loss?

options.feedback: In the stated toy model, a larger gain is needed to match the felt weight of the loss.
Ten matches the point loss. In this model, that loss feels twice as strong.
Fewer points could not balance a loss that feels twice as strong. It takes 20 gained points here.

items.stem: A teacher says either “you keep five points” or “you lose five points.” The final score is the same. What changed?

options.feedback: Calling it keeping or losing changes the starting point you feel, even though the final score stays the same.
The word lose can feel like more is at stake. Both lines still name five points.
Both lines end at the same score. Only the frame, keep or lose, has changed.

items.stem: Two offers end with the same money. One is described as losing part of what you have. Why does that one feel worse?

options.text: Losing from what you hold feels heavier.
options.feedback: A drop from what is held can weigh more than an equal gain from another starting point.
The end sum looks like the whole story. The starting point can change how it feels.

options.text: Same money must feel the same.
options.feedback: The end sums match, so equal feelings seem likely. The frame can still change felt value.

items.stem: We judge a result against where we started. Ending up below the start feels like a ___.

options.feedback: The starting point is key: the same final amount can feel like a gain or like a loss.
Missing a hoped-for result can feel disappointing. But here, a loss means ending below where you started.
A fresh start is not what this pattern describes. Ending below where you started is felt as a loss.

items.stem: A coach says every player will feel a loss exactly twice as much as a win. What is wrong?

options.text: That is an average; people differ.
options.feedback: People differ. The study shows a common trend, not one set amount for every person.

options.text: Every player must feel losses more.
options.feedback: The group trend is strong, so this sounds safe. It does not set each player's feeling.

options.text: A group average sets each person's feeling.
options.feedback: A group average is easy to reuse. It does not set how each player feels.

items.stem: You start with ten tokens. Match each change to what it is.

options.feedback: Moving above the start adds one token, so it belongs on the gain side.
One extra token sits above the start, so its sign is positive in this example.
The end count sits below the same start, making this a loss of one token.
The number fell by one; its felt weight may still differ from an equal gain.

misconceptions.name: Equal feel
misconceptions.correction: Equal gain and loss can have a different felt weight.

misconceptions.name: Always true
misconceptions.correction: The pattern does not fix how every person will feel.

quest.title: Frame a token
quest.detail: Write a made-up choice as a gain and then as a loss from a starting point. Ask how the frame may shift its feel.

steps.title: A loss feels bigger than a gain

hook.stem: A friend offers a coin toss: heads you win ₹100, tails you pay ₹100. Do most people take it?

options.feedback: Right. Most people turn down a fair bet like this. Paying ₹100 feels bigger than winning ₹100.
It is fair on paper, but most people still say no. Paying ₹100 feels worse than winning ₹100 feels good.

options.text: Only people who dislike games say no.
options.feedback: Most people say no, not just a few. A drop tends to weigh more than a gain of the same size.

steps.teach: A loss often feels stronger than a gain of the same size. This is called loss aversion.

parts: Sahil finds ₹50 on the bus and smiles for a minute, but when ₹50 falls out of his pocket,
he is upset all evening.
example.spot: he is upset all evening.
example.feedback: The same ₹50 felt much bigger as a drop than as a find.

guided.stem: In a hostel game, Varun has 10 points. Giving up 2 points upsets him more than winning 2 points pleases him. What does this show?
guided.hint: Compare a drop and a gain of the same size.

options.text: A drop weighs more than a gain.
options.feedback: Yes. The same 2 points feel bigger as a drop than as a gain.

options.text: He does not care about points.
options.feedback: He clearly cares. The drop just feels stronger than the gain.
Here it is the other way round. The drop feels stronger.

guided.stem: In a cricket match, Anjali’s team gets 5 lucky runs, then gives away 5 runs from a bad throw. Which moment stays with her longer?
guided.hint: Which feels stronger: a gain or a drop of the same size?

options.feedback: Right. A drop often feels stronger than a gain of the same size.
The gain is nice, but a drop of the same size tends to weigh more.

options.text: Both stay with her the same.
options.feedback: The runs are the same, but a drop tends to feel bigger than a gain.

steps.takeaway: A loss tends to feel bigger than a gain of the same size.

steps.title: It depends on where you start

hook.stem: Riya hoped for ₹500 from her aunt and got ₹300. Ravi hoped for nothing and got ₹300. Who feels better?

options.feedback: Right. Ravi hoped for nothing, so ₹300 is a gain. Riya hoped for ₹500, so ₹300 feels like a drop.
Riya hoped for ₹500, so ₹300 feels ₹200 short. Ravi hoped for nothing, so it is all gain.

options.text: Both feel the same, since both got ₹300.
options.feedback: The amount is the same, but the starting points differ. We judge from where we start.

steps.teach: We judge a result by where we start or what we expect. The same ₹300 can feel like a gain or a loss.

parts: Meghna and Kunal both end the month with ₹1,000, but
Meghna started with ₹1,500,
so her month feels like a loss.
example.spot: Meghna started with ₹1,500,
example.feedback: Her start point was higher, so the same ₹1,000 feels like a drop.

guided.stem: In an exam, Pranav hoped for 90 and got 80. Neha hoped for 70 and got 80. Who is more pleased?
guided.hint: Compare each score with what each one hoped for.

options.feedback: Yes. For Neha, 80 is above her start point, so it feels like a gain.
Pranav hoped for 90, so 80 feels like a drop for him.

options.text: Both, since the score is the same.
options.feedback: The score is the same, but their start points differ.

guided.stem: One canteen says “Pay ₹5 extra by card.” Another says “Get ₹5 off with cash.” The prices end up the same. What differs?
guided.hint: Look at the start price each one names.

options.text: Only the start point in the wording.
options.feedback: Right. One frames card as a loss, the other frames cash as a gain.
The money ends up the same. Only the framing changed.
The money is the same, but the frame changes how it feels.

steps.takeaway: Gain or loss depends on where you start.

concepts.title: Anchoring
concepts.hook: A random number can pull a later estimate: the first figure matters even when it has no link to the answer.
concepts.rule: An early number can pull a later guess toward it. That first number may be useful or random, so the guess needs a check beyond the anchor.

claims.text: A first number can pull a later guess toward it.
An anchor can pull a guess even when the first number is arbitrary.

items.stem: A shop tag shows ₹900 crossed out, then ₹600. What sways your guess of a fair price?

options.feedback: An early figure can pull a later judgment before any outside price is checked.
The cut looks large. That first tag is set by the seller, not an outside check.
The current price looks like the obvious clue, but the first ₹900 tag can pull the guess about a fair price.

items.stem: Two friends guess the cost of a school trip. One first hears ₹2,000, the other ₹8,000. What happens to their guesses?

options.feedback: Each guess can start near the first number heard. The numbers may have been made up.

options.text: They match, since it is the same trip.
options.feedback: Both guess the same trip cost, so matching guesses seem likely. Their first numbers differ.
Studies show a heard number can tug a guess, even a random one. Their first guesses may drift apart.

items.stem: In a study, people saw a random first number, 65, before guessing a percentage. What was their typical guess?

options.feedback: The high number pulled guesses up. The typical guess in the group shown the low number was 25%.
The 65% card was vivid, so it is easy to reuse. The typical guess in that group was 45%.
That was the typical guess after the low number. People shown 65% gave a typical guess of 45%.

items.stem: A pen's old price is crossed out and cut. How can you tell if it is really cheap?

options.text: Check the same pen at another shop.
options.feedback: A second shop's price gives a fresh clue that the first tag cannot give.
The old tag looks like a bargain clue. The seller may have set it high.

options.text: Look at how big the sale sticker is.
options.feedback: A big sticker is still set by the seller. A price for the same pen elsewhere gives an outside check.

items.stem: Students are told a number is random. They see 65, then guess a percentage. Why do guesses still drift toward 65?

options.text: They start from the first number and adjust.
options.feedback: The first number can pull later guesses, even when it gives no real clue.

options.text: Knowing it is random stops the pull.
options.feedback: The warning should help. Yet people can still start near the first number they saw.

options.text: A random number is a fair clue.
options.feedback: It appeared right before the question, so it can feel relevant. The number was random.

items.stem: Riya sees a number on a poster, then guesses close to it. That first number is an ___.

options.feedback: The first number can tug a guess, even if the poster gives no real clue.
A printed figure looks official. It is the first cue, not an outside check.
The figure was not worked out from many guesses. It is simply the first number heard, so it acts as an anchor.

items.stem: A seller crosses out ₹500 and asks ₹300. A buyer says the old tag proves it is a good deal. What is wrong?

options.text: The seller chose that old number.
options.feedback: The crossed-out tag can pull the guess, even though it says nothing about what the item is worth elsewhere.

options.text: A big cut always means a good deal.
options.feedback: The cut price catches the eye. A price from another seller is a better check.

options.text: The old tag proves value on its own.
options.feedback: Two tags look like two prices. Both came from the same seller, so neither is an outside check.

items.stem: Which line explains anchoring best?

options.text: The first number you hear pulls your guess.
options.feedback: Even a made-up first number can pull a later guess toward it.

options.text: The latest number wipes out the first.
options.feedback: The latest number feels fresh. The first one can still tug the later guess.

options.text: A guess is right if it matches the first number.
options.feedback: Matching the first number does not make a guess right. That number may have been random.

misconceptions.name: First means fair
misconceptions.correction: The first number is not proof of the fair value.

misconceptions.name: Random has no pull
misconceptions.correction: Even an arbitrary first number can sway a later guess.

quest.title: Compare tags
quest.detail: Pick two made-up price tags. Start a guess from each, then see how the first number may pull the guess.

steps.title: A first number pulls your guess

hook.stem: A seller first says a kurta costs ₹2,000, then offers it for ₹1,200. Why does ₹1,200 seem cheap?

options.feedback: Right. The first number set the starting point for your sense of the price.

options.text: ₹1,200 is always low for a kurta.
options.feedback: Not always. It seems low mainly because ₹2,000 came first.
Sellers can start at any number. The first one still pulls your sense of the price.

steps.teach: The first number you see can pull your later guess toward it. That first number is called an anchor.

parts: Rohit hears “50,000” on TV,
then guesses that 45,000 people fit in the stadium.
example.spot: Rohit hears “50,000” on TV,
example.feedback: The TV number came first and pulled his guess close to it.

guided.stem: At a fair, a stall shows ₹800 for a bag, then cuts it to ₹500. What is the anchor?
guided.hint: The anchor is the number you see first.

options.feedback: Yes. The ₹800 came first and makes ₹500 look small.
That is the final price. The anchor is the first number, ₹800.

options.text: What the bag is really worth.
options.feedback: Its real worth is not shown here. The anchor is the first number shown.

guided.stem: Before guessing how long a train trip takes, Kavya’s friend says “maybe 10 hours.” Kavya guesses 9. Why so close to 10?
guided.hint: Which number did she hear first?

options.text: Her friend’s number pulled her guess.
options.feedback: Right. The first number she heard acted as an anchor.
She did not check anything. Her friend’s number came first and pulled her guess.
Trip times vary. Her guess sat near the first number she heard.

steps.takeaway: The first number you hear can steer your guess.

steps.title: Even a random number pulls

hook.stem: People spin a wheel that lands on a random number, then guess a fact. Does the random number change their guess?

options.feedback: Right. In a classic study, even a number from a wheel pulled guesses toward it.
People try to, but in studies the random number still pulled their guesses.

options.text: Only if the number is very large.
options.feedback: In the classic study, both a high and a low random number pulled guesses.

steps.teach: Even a random number can pull a guess. People start from it and do not move far enough away.

visual.label: Typical guess of a percentage after a random number

parts: Arnav writes down his roll number, which ends in 90,
then guesses that a canteen thali costs ₹90.
example.spot: Arnav writes down his roll number, which ends in 90,
example.feedback: His roll number has nothing to do with the thali, yet it pulled his guess.

guided.stem: Before a GK quiz, a screen flashes a random number, 900. Then Tara guesses a tower is 800 metres tall. Why so high?
guided.hint: Did the first number have any link to the tower?

options.text: The random number pulled her guess up.
options.feedback: Yes. Even a number with no link can pull a guess toward it.
She was guessing. The random 900 pulled her guess up.
In studies they did. People start from the number and move too little.

guided.stem: One cricket team sees a random 12 on the board, another sees 2. Then both guess how many sixes a match will have. Who guesses higher?
guided.hint: Each group starts from the number it saw.

options.feedback: Right. A higher first number tends to pull guesses higher.
A low number tends to pull guesses down, not up.
In studies, groups that saw different numbers gave different guesses.

steps.takeaway: Even a made-up number can tug your guess toward it.

concepts.title: Confirmation bias
concepts.hook: In Wason's card task, most people turned a card that could prove the rule right and skipped the one that could prove it wrong.
concepts.rule: Confirmation bias is a pull to seek or notice clues that fit a belief. A fair test also looks for clues that could show the belief is wrong.

claims.text: People can focus on clues that fit a prior belief while missing other clues.
A test of an idea is stronger when it can find a case that goes against it.

items.stem: Aditi thinks every hard exam has a trick in it. Which papers does she recall most?

options.text: The ones with a trick question.
options.feedback: A matching case fits her belief and may stand out more than a plain paper.
A paper with no trick is easy to set aside. It could test her claim that all have one.

options.text: Papers she has not taken yet.
options.feedback: A paper not yet taken is no memory at all. The bias shows in how trick papers stand out when she looks back.

items.stem: A family shop owner thinks rain always cuts sales. Which days should she check to test that?

options.text: Rainy days when sales held up.
options.feedback: A possible exception can show whether the word “always” holds up across the records.
A wet slow day fits her view. Rainy days with steady sales could test it better.

options.text: Only dry days with high sales.
options.feedback: Dry days say little about the rain claim. Rainy days with steady sales are the records that test it.

items.stem: In one card puzzle, people had to pick the cards that could test a rule and prove it wrong. About what percent got it right?

options.feedback: Only a few people chose both cards needed to check whether the rule could be broken.
The large share left over seems close. Only 16% chose the key pair.
Half is a natural guess, but far fewer found it. Only 16% chose the pair that could disprove the rule.

items.stem: A fan says a batter always flops in run chases. Which innings would show that is not true?

options.feedback: One clear case that breaks it is enough to disprove a claim that says “always.”
A poor chase fits the fan's view. One good chase could break the word always.
An overall average mixes chases with other games. One good chase innings is what breaks the word always.

items.stem: Someone claims every late bus is red. Why check a late bus that is not red?

options.text: One could prove the claim wrong.
options.feedback: A red late bus fits the rule, but one late bus of another colour would break it.

options.text: A red late bus proves it for all.
options.feedback: A match feels like proof. One late bus of another colour would break the rule.

options.text: Lots of red buses outweigh it.
options.feedback: A single late bus of another colour would break the rule, no matter how many red matches were found.

items.stem: Sana keeps only the screenshots that agree with her guess. Her pile is tilted toward ___.

options.feedback: The pattern can make a weak idea seem stronger by hiding cases that point away.

options.text: A tested idea, since she found matches.
options.feedback: A few matches can feel like proof. Yet the skipped cases may show the guess is wrong.
Picking only matching screenshots is the opposite of random. She keeps what fits and drops the rest.

items.stem: Priya keeps three bus logs that fit her belief and drops two that do not. She calls it proven. What is wrong?

options.text: She left out the logs that disagree.
options.feedback: Selecting only matches can make a weak belief look stronger than the full record supports.
Saved cases feel clear and close at hand. The skipped logs can test the belief too.

options.text: Three logs beat any dropped ones.
options.feedback: Three saved matches look strong. The skipped logs may be the cases that break the claim.

items.stem: How can someone miss clues that go against their belief?

options.text: We notice what fits and skip the rest.
options.feedback: The bias is in what we look for and remember, whether the first idea is true or not.

options.text: A strong belief makes all clues easy to recall.
options.feedback: Memory can feel fair. Yet we may recall what fits our view and miss what does not.

options.text: Only people with weak beliefs miss clues.
options.feedback: Strong and weak beliefs can both steer what we notice. The bias is lopsided searching, not how strong the belief is.

misconceptions.name: One match proves it
misconceptions.correction: One fitting case may fit more than one idea.

misconceptions.name: Disproof is useless
misconceptions.correction: A case against an idea can test it well.

sources.title: Problem Solving, Psychology 2e
Motivated Reasoning and Performance on the Wason Selection Task
sources.publisher: Dawson, Gilovich and Regan, Personality and Social Psychology Bulletin

quest.title: Try to disprove
quest.detail: Pick a low-stakes belief about a game or bus. Write one clue that could show it is wrong.

steps.title: We notice what fits

hook.stem: Mohit thinks his lucky pen helps in exams. Which exams does he recall best?

options.text: The ones that went well with the pen.
options.feedback: Right. Cases that fit a belief stand out. The others fade from view.

options.text: Every exam, good and bad, the same.
options.feedback: Memory is not that even. Cases that fit his belief stand out more.

options.text: The ones that went badly with the pen.
options.feedback: Those go against his belief, so they tend to get less notice.

steps.teach: People notice and recall clues that fit what they already believe, and skip the rest. This is called confirmation bias.

parts: Zara thinks Mondays are unlucky, so
she writes down every bad Monday and skips the good ones.
example.spot: she writes down every bad Monday and skips the good ones.
example.feedback: She keeps only the cases that fit her belief, so it looks stronger than it is.

guided.stem: Arjun thinks one shopkeeper is rude. He recalls two rude moments, not the ten polite ones. What is going on?
guided.hint: Which moments fit his belief?

options.text: He notices what fits his belief.
options.feedback: Yes. The rude moments fit, so they stand out.
The ten polite moments say otherwise. He just recalls the ones that fit.
His memory works. It just picks out the moments that fit his belief.

guided.stem: Sneha thinks her team plays better in white jerseys. She only looks up the matches they won in white. What is missing?
guided.hint: What about the matches that do not fit?

options.text: The matches in white they did not win.
options.feedback: Right. Those could go against her idea, so they matter too.
More matches that fit will not test the idea. She needs the ones that do not fit.

options.text: Nothing, since the wins prove it.
options.feedback: Wins alone show only the cases that fit. The other cases are missing.

steps.takeaway: We see what fits our belief and skip what does not.

steps.title: Test with a case that could break it

hook.stem: A friend says every crow is black. What would test that claim best?

options.text: Looking for a crow that is not black.
options.feedback: Right. One crow of another colour would break the claim. That is a strong test.
Each black crow fits, but it cannot show the claim is wrong. A strong test looks for one that breaks it.
Agreement is not a test. A crow of another colour would be.

steps.teach: A strong test looks for a case that could show the idea is wrong. One clear exception can break a claim that says “always.”

right.title: Strong test
lines: Look for a case that breaks it

example.ask: Tap the test that could break his idea.
parts: To test his idea that the 8 o’clock bus is always late,
Farhan looks for a day it came on time.
example.spot: Farhan looks for a day it came on time.
example.feedback: One on-time day would break “always late,” so it is a strong test.

guided.stem: Dev says phones that cost more always have better cameras. Which phone could prove him wrong?
guided.hint: Look for a case that breaks the “always.”

options.text: A costly phone with a weak camera.
options.feedback: Yes. One such phone would break his claim.

options.text: A costly phone with a great camera.
options.feedback: That fits his claim, so it cannot prove it wrong.

options.text: A cheap phone with a weak camera.
options.feedback: That fits too. Only a costly phone with a weak camera would break it.

guided.stem: Pooja thinks music while studying always lowers her marks. What would test this best?
guided.hint: Which result would go against her idea?

options.text: A test where she did well with music on.
options.feedback: Right. A good result with music would go against her idea.

options.text: Recalling low marks with music on.
options.feedback: Those fit her idea, so they cannot test it well.
Views are not a test. A result that goes against the idea is.

steps.takeaway: To test an idea, look for the case that could break it.

concepts.title: Social proof
concepts.hook: In Asch's line test, a group giving a plainly wrong answer still pulled some people away from what they could see.
concepts.rule: A crowd choice can act as a clue and pull a person’s choice. But a crowd can be wrong; group agreement is not proof.

claims.text: In Asch’s line task, group answers sometimes pulled a person toward a wrong answer.
Group agreement is social input, not proof that a claim is true.
Seeing what many others choose can lean a person’s own choice toward it.
A group can agree on a wrong answer, so agreement alone is a clue, not proof.

items.stem: At a hostel quiz, most students call out the wrong line as longest. What happens to the last student's answer?

options.text: It often moves toward the group.
options.feedback: When everyone answers out loud, the group can change some answers, even on an easy task.

options.text: A clear task keeps it fully their own.
options.feedback: The line looks clear, so a solo choice seems safe. Some people still followed the wrong group.

options.text: It moves away from the group on purpose.
options.feedback: Some people do resist, but few go against a group just to differ. The pull tends to run toward the group.

items.stem: At a cricket watch party, everyone cheers a close call before the replay. What do the cheers do?

options.text: Make the call feel more certain.
options.feedback: The cheers come first. They can sway a guess before the replay gives a clear view.
The crowd sounds sure, so the call may feel settled. The replay can still show it was wrong.
Cheers cannot change the footage. They can only make the call feel more certain before the replay.

items.stem: In a famous test, a group gave the same wrong answer out loud. About what percent of the time did the one real person go along?

options.feedback: Asch reported 36.8% wrong answers on critical trials, showing a strong group pull.
One percent sounds right for an easy line task. The wrong group pulled far more answers.
About three in four people went along at least once. Of all critical answers, about 37% followed the wrong group.

items.stem: A whole class picks the same answer to an easy puzzle. What does that alone tell you?

options.text: They agree, not that they are right.
options.feedback: The group may share a mistake, so a headcount alone cannot settle the visual fact.
A full class can look like proof. They may share the same wrong cue.
Shared answers do not prove cheating either. Agreement by itself cannot settle whether the answer is right.

items.stem: Nisha can clearly see which line matches. She still says the group's wrong answer out loud. Why?

options.text: Fitting in can beat what she sees.
options.feedback: In Asch’s task, public group pressure could pull answers away from the visible line lengths.

options.text: Votes cannot sway a clear answer.
options.feedback: The lines look clear, so this sounds likely. Group pressure can still shift a public answer.

options.text: The group's vote proves her eyes wrong.
options.feedback: A group that all agrees can seem more trustworthy than one person. But their votes can sway an answer without changing the lines.

items.stem: When a crowd's choice nudges your own choice, the crowd works as a ___.

options.feedback: The signal comes from what others did, though its size does not make it reliable.
Many votes look like many checks. The votes can sway one another.
A crowd's choice is not an answer key. It works as a social cue, which can still be wrong.

items.stem: A group picks B before anyone checks. A student says everyone agrees, so it is proven. What is wrong?

options.text: They may have copied each other.
options.feedback: A shared answer can spread through a group, so agreement alone is not a fresh check.

options.text: More votes make an answer true.
options.feedback: A crowd can feel like strong proof. Its size does not fix a wrong answer.

options.text: All agreeing means each one checked.
options.feedback: All the votes match, so they look like separate choices. But the first answer may have shaped the rest.

items.stem: What did the famous line test show?

options.text: A wrong group sometimes swayed people.
options.feedback: The finding shows influence in that setting, while people did not all copy every time.
A strong group pull sounds like it works every time. Some people kept their own answer.

options.text: Nobody was swayed by the group.
options.feedback: Many answers on the test rounds did follow the wrong group. The pull was real, though not total.

misconceptions.name: Crowd proves truth
misconceptions.correction: A group can agree on a wrong answer.

misconceptions.name: No one is swayed
misconceptions.correction: Group answers can pull some people in some settings.

sources.title: Conformity, Compliance, and Obedience, Psychology 2e
Opinions and Social Pressure

quest.title: Watch a group cue
quest.detail: In a harmless choice, note whether a visible group choice changes a guess. Keep the check kind.

steps.title: A crowd’s choice is a clue

hook.stem: In class, everyone around you raises a hand for answer B. You thought A. What do you feel pulled to do?

options.feedback: Right. When many people pick one answer, it pulls on our own choice.
Usually the pull goes the other way, toward the group’s answer.

options.text: Nothing, since others do not matter.
options.feedback: Others do matter. A group answer can pull our own.

steps.teach: What a crowd picks works as a clue, so our own choice leans toward it. This is called social proof.

parts: At the canteen,
Neel sees everyone order the masala dosa,
so he orders it too, though he came for idli.
example.spot: Neel sees everyone order the masala dosa,
example.feedback: What everyone else ordered acted as a clue and pulled his choice.

guided.stem: In a class poll, most students vote for a Sunday trip. Aisha was leaning to Saturday, but she votes Sunday. What pulled her?
guided.hint: What did she see before she voted?

options.feedback: Yes. The group’s choice worked as a clue and pulled hers.
Nothing in the story is about weather. The votes she saw came first.

options.text: A rule that she must agree.
options.feedback: There is no such rule. The group’s votes pulled her choice.

guided.stem: A song has 10 crore views. Before playing it, Bhavna already expects it to be good. Why?
guided.hint: What does the view count tell her about other people?

options.feedback: Right. The crowd’s choice works as a clue about the song.
She has not played it yet. The view count is the clue.
Nothing says she does. The view count is what shaped her guess.

steps.takeaway: What a crowd picks can pull your own pick.

steps.title: Even a wrong crowd can pull

hook.stem: In a test, a group gives a plainly wrong answer about line lengths. How often did the one real person go along?

options.text: About a third of the time.
options.feedback: Right. In Asch’s test, people went along with the wrong group in about 37% of answers.

options.text: Never, since the answer was so plain.
options.feedback: Alone, people almost never got it wrong. With a wrong group, they went along about a third of the time.
Not that often. People went along in about 37% of answers, and some never did.

steps.teach: When a group gives a plainly wrong answer, some people go along. In Asch’s line test, this happened in about a third of answers.

visual.label: Wrong answers in Asch’s line test

parts: Every student before Tanya calls the shorter line the longest, and
Tanya says the same,
though she can see it is wrong.
example.spot: Tanya says the same,
example.feedback: She can see the right answer, yet the group’s wrong answer pulls her along.

guided.stem: In a hostel quiz, five friends say Delhi is south of Chennai. Kabir knows it is not, but he nods. What is going on?
guided.hint: What did the group do before Kabir answered?

options.text: The wrong group pulled him along.
options.feedback: Yes. A group can pull someone toward a wrong answer, even a plain one.

options.text: He changed his mind about the map.
options.feedback: He still knows the map. The group’s pull made him nod.

options.text: He did not hear the question.
options.feedback: He heard it. The group’s wrong answer is what pulled him.

guided.stem: In a music class, everyone calls a note higher than it is. Anu hears it clearly but agrees. Does everyone act like Anu?
guided.hint: In Asch’s test, did every person go along?

options.text: No, some stay with what they hear.
options.feedback: Right. In Asch’s test, about a quarter of people never went along.
Not everyone. In Asch’s test, about a quarter never went along.
Some people do. In Asch’s test, wrong answers came in about a third of tries.

steps.takeaway: A group can pull us toward an answer we can see is wrong.

steps.title: Agreement is not proof

hook.stem: Thirty classmates forward the same message saying the exam is moved. Does that make it true?

options.text: No, they may all be sharing one message.
options.feedback: Right. Many people agreeing is not a fresh check of the fact.

options.text: Yes, so many people cannot be wrong.
options.feedback: A group can share one mistake. In Asch’s test, groups agreed on a wrong answer.

options.text: Yes, if they are all friends.
options.feedback: Friends can share a mistake too. Agreement is not proof.

steps.teach: A crowd can agree on a wrong answer. Many people saying the same thing is a clue, not proof.

parts: Everyone in the hostel says the mess serves paneer on Friday, but
when Sid checks the menu, it says Thursday.
example.spot: when Sid checks the menu, it says Thursday.
example.feedback: Everyone agreed, yet the menu was the real check, and it showed they were wrong.

guided.stem: In a group project, everyone agrees the answer is 42 without working it out. What does their agreement show?
guided.hint: Did anyone check the working?

options.feedback: Yes. Agreement is not a check. The working would be.
Not yet. A group can agree on a wrong answer.
It may be right or wrong. Agreement alone does not tell us.

guided.stem: A whole cricket crowd says the ball crossed the rope. What would settle whether it was a six?
guided.hint: What is a fresh check, apart from the crowd?

options.feedback: Right. The replay is a real check. The crowd’s view is only a clue.
Loud agreement is still just agreement. The replay checks the fact.

options.text: How many fans posted about it.
options.feedback: More posts are not more proof. The replay is the real check.

steps.takeaway: Many people agreeing is a clue, not proof.

concepts.title: The planning fallacy
concepts.hook: In a study, students thought their papers would take less time than they did. Even their best guesses ran short.
concepts.rule: The planning fallacy is a tilt toward a short time guess for our own task. Looking at past tasks and missed steps can give a better time guess.

claims.text: People can underguess how long their own tasks will take.
Plans can miss delays that happened in similar past work.
In one study, linking past tasks to a new plan made the too-short guesses go away.
When people plan, they tend to picture the task going smoothly and leave delays out of the guess.

items.stem: A hostel team says its chart will take one hour. They forgot about printing. What happens?

options.text: It takes longer than they guessed.
options.feedback: Leaving a step out of the plan in your head makes the finish-time guess too short.

options.text: Printing does not count as work.
options.feedback: The chart may be done in an hour. It still takes time to print and finish.
One hour is the team's clear target. It still leaves out print work.

items.stem: In exam week, Isha plans a revision sheet but forgets she must find past papers first. Which guess is now too short?

options.text: Her guess of when she will finish.
options.feedback: The missing collection step adds work outside the smooth path she pictured.
Writing feels like the main task, but collecting papers is another step and can make the whole plan take longer.
Marking happens after she finishes. The missed step changes her own finish-time guess.

items.stem: A club plans posters in 2 hours. Past posters took 3, 4 and 5 hours. What is a better guess?

options.feedback: Past posters averaged four hours, and that time includes steps the new plan left out.
Two hours is the team's own guess. Past posters took three to five hours.
That was the longest past job, not the typical one. The average of 3, 4 and 5 is 4 hours.

items.stem: Sara plans time only for drawing her poster. What else needs time?

options.text: Time to find and print images.
options.feedback: Finding and printing images take time beyond the drawing step she counted.
Counting the same drawing time again does not cover the tasks she left out.
A poster needs more than drawing. Finding and printing images add time the plan left out.

items.stem: A team pictures a smooth poster project and ignores printing delays. Why is their time guess too short?

options.feedback: The best-case picture leaves out printing time, which real tasks like this often include.

options.text: Printing is too small to matter.
options.feedback: It can look like a quick last step. Past tasks show such work still takes time.

options.text: A smooth plan makes extra steps free.
options.feedback: The planned parts may go well. The print step still takes time even then.

items.stem: To guess how long a new task will take, look at how long old tasks ___.

options.feedback: Old jobs show the time used, with snags and steps the new plan may miss.
Old plans are easy to compare. Old finish times show what the work took.
A snag-free time is just another hopeful guess. The real time old tasks took includes the delays.

items.stem: Past posters took four to six hours. A new plan says one hour because the art is ready. Printing is not counted. What is wrong?

options.text: It skips printing and ignores past times.
options.feedback: Ready artwork may help, yet the past tasks and missing printing step still matter.

options.text: The new plan makes the past times useless.
options.feedback: The ready art is a real change. Yet past times can still flag missed tasks such as print.

options.text: Ready art makes other steps disappear.
options.feedback: Ready art does save time. It does not make print and other steps vanish.

items.stem: Which sentence sums up the planning fallacy?

options.text: We picture a smooth path, so we guess too little time.
options.feedback: Past completed jobs can reveal delays that a new plan has not pictured.

options.text: Every late job comes from a bad plan.
options.feedback: A late job can look like a bad plan. This idea is about time guesses, not every delay.
The idea is not about plan length. It is about guessing too little time for our own task.

misconceptions.name: Best case is normal
misconceptions.correction: A smooth plan is only one path; delays can add time.

misconceptions.name: Past tasks do not help
misconceptions.correction: Past task times can show steps a new plan has missed.

sources.title: Exploring the Planning Fallacy: Why People Underestimate Their Task Completion Times
sources.publisher: Buehler, Griffin and Ross, Journal of Personality and Social Psychology

quest.title: Time a small task
quest.detail: Before a small school task, note a time guess. Afterward, note the time and one step the guess missed.

steps.title: We guess too little time

hook.stem: Students guessed when they would finish a big college project. How did their guesses compare with the real time?

options.feedback: Right. On average they guessed 34 days and took about 56.
They were far off. They guessed 34 days on average and took about 56.
The other way round. On average, they took longer than they guessed.

steps.teach: Guesses for our own tasks often fall short; this is the planning fallacy. In one study, students took about 56 days for a thesis they guessed would take 34.

visual.label: Days to finish a thesis, in one study

parts: Ishan says his science model will take one evening,
but three evenings later he is still gluing parts.
example.spot: but three evenings later he is still gluing parts.
example.feedback: His guess was far too short. That is the planning fallacy.

guided.stem: Priya guesses her essay will take 2 hours. It takes 5. What does this show?
guided.hint: Was her guess too long or too short?

options.feedback: Yes. Guessing too short for our own task is very common.
Speed is not the point. Her guess for her own task was too short.
Times vary. The point is that her own guess was too short.

guided.stem: Aman plans to clean his hostel room in 20 minutes. It takes an hour. Why is this common?
guided.hint: Think about guesses for our own tasks.

options.text: People often guess short for their own tasks.
options.feedback: Right. We tend to guess too little time for our own tasks.
The room did not grow messier. His guess was just too short.
Effort is not the issue. Short guesses for our own tasks are common.

steps.takeaway: Your own tasks often take longer than you guess.

steps.title: We picture a smooth path

hook.stem: Kunal plans to print his project in 10 minutes. What might his plan leave out?

options.text: The queue at the print shop.
options.feedback: Right. Plans often picture a smooth path and leave out delays like a queue.
Printing is quick, but getting it done can hit delays, like a queue.
That will not change the time much. Delays like a queue will.

steps.teach: When we plan, we picture the task going smoothly. Delays and extra steps get left out of the guess.

example.ask: Tap the step she left out.
parts: Ritu plans her poster as draw, then colour, but
she forgets the trip to buy chart paper.
example.spot: she forgets the trip to buy chart paper.
example.feedback: The shop trip is a step her smooth plan left out.

guided.stem: Harsh plans to reach the station in 15 minutes. He did not think about traffic. What is his plan missing?
guided.hint: What could slow him on the way?

options.feedback: Yes. A smooth plan often leaves out delays like traffic.
The gap in the plan is not the bike. It left out delays.
Maybe on a clear road. His plan did not count delays like traffic.

guided.stem: Sanya plans to cook dinner in 30 minutes. She forgets she must first buy vegetables. What did she leave out?
guided.hint: Which step comes before cooking?

options.feedback: Right. Her plan pictured only the cooking and left out a step.
That comes after dinner. The missing step comes before cooking.
That takes little time. The shop trip is the big missed step.

steps.takeaway: A smooth plan leaves out the delays.

steps.title: Past tasks give a better guess

hook.stem: Your last three lab reports took 2, 3 and 4 hours. A new one is due. What is a fair time guess?

options.feedback: Right. Your past reports are a real guide, and they took about 3 hours.

options.text: About 1 hour, if all goes well.
options.feedback: That pictures a smooth path. Past reports took 2 to 4 hours.

options.text: There is no way to guess.
options.feedback: There is. Past reports took 2 to 4 hours, so about 3 is fair.

steps.teach: How long similar tasks really took is a good guide. In one study, linking past tasks to a new plan made the too-short guesses go away.

nodes: Link them to the new task

example.ask: Tap the past tasks he uses.
parts: Before guessing,
Yash recalls that his last two speeches took a week to prepare,
so he plans a week again.
example.spot: Yash recalls that his last two speeches took a week to prepare,
example.feedback: He links past tasks to the new one, which gives a better guess.

guided.stem: Leela’s past sketches each took about 3 hours. Her plan for a new sketch says 1 hour. Which guess is likely closer?
guided.hint: What did similar tasks really take?

options.feedback: Yes. Her past sketches are a better guide than a hopeful plan.
That is the hopeful plan. Her past sketches took about 3 hours.
Nothing points to 10. Her past sketches took about 3 hours.

guided.stem: A cricket club’s last two match teas took 2 hours to set up. This time they plan 30 minutes. What would give a better guess?
guided.hint: Look at what happened before.

options.feedback: Right. Past setups show the real time, delays and all.
Hope is the smooth plan. Past setups show the real time.
A new guess may also picture a smooth path. Past setups are the better guide.

steps.takeaway: Past tasks show how long the next one may take.

concepts.title: Sleep and memory
concepts.hook: New learning can become more stable during sleep, even without another round of practice.
concepts.rule: Sleep supports the later strengthening and organising of some new memories; it does not replace learning in the first place.

claims.text: Studies find that sleep after learning can help later recall.
Sleep can help new memories in many tasks. Quiet rest can help too.
After you learn, a new memory can get firm over time. This is called consolidation.

items.stem: In the hostel, Kiran learns a short poem, then sleeps. What happens to the memory overnight?

options.feedback: In some tests, sleep after study helps people recall more later.
No new lines are practiced during sleep, so it can seem idle. Sleep can help stabilise what was learned earlier.
Sleep does not wipe new memories. In some studies, sleep after learning helps people recall more later.

items.stem: In exam week, Rohan reads a chapter once, then sleeps. Which part is the actual learning?

options.feedback: The material first has to be encoded before later processing can help keep it.
Sleep can help keep what was read. But the first step was to read it.
Waking is not when learning starts. Reading the chapter is the first step that puts it in memory.

items.stem: In a small sleep study, people recalled 20.4 word pairs after sleep and 12.6 after staying awake. About what percent better was sleep?

options.feedback: The difference is 7.75 pairs. Divide by the wake score, 12.63, to get about 61%. This was one small study.
Dividing 7.75 by the sleep score uses the larger group as the base. Compared with wake recall, the gain was about 61%.
Both groups learned pairs, but after 12 hours this study found higher recall after sleep.

items.stem: Meena learns a poem and remembers it better the next day. What helped it last?

options.feedback: After the first lesson, the brain can help keep the new memory over time.
Reading starts the trace. The question asks what can strengthen it after that first encounter.
Losing the poem would make recall worse, not better. The step after learning that helps a memory last is called consolidation.

items.stem: Dev practises a skill, sleeps, and does better the next day. How could sleep help?

options.text: The brain keeps working on new practice.
options.feedback: Sleep can aid recall. One test alone does not show each brain step.

options.text: Sleep teaches the skill without practice.
options.feedback: Better recall after sleep can look like new learning. The skill was first learned during practice.

options.text: Sleep plays no part; it is all practice.
options.feedback: Practice came first, so it is easy to credit it all. Sleep may also help keep a new skill.

items.stem: First you learn a word. Later the memory gets steadier. That later step is called ___.

options.feedback: It names changes after initial learning that can help the word remain available.
The first sight of the word matters. The gap asks for what helps keep it later.
A memory that gets steadier is not fading. The later step that firms it up is called consolidation.

items.stem: A friend says memories only get stronger while you sleep. What is wrong?

options.text: Quiet rest while awake helps too.
options.feedback: Sleep plays a big part, but studies also find gains after quiet rest with few distractions.
Sleep has a known role, so this seems likely. Waking rest can help as well.

options.text: Only sleep can change a memory.
options.feedback: Sleep gets more notice in memory studies. Quiet rest can also help new learning last.

items.stem: Which line sums up sleep and learning?

options.text: Sleep can help keep what was learned.
options.feedback: It can help keep what was learned. It does not teach new facts alone.

options.text: Sleep can teach a chapter you never read.
options.feedback: Sleep can help after study, so it may sound like a teacher. The chapter must be read first.
Sleep helps keep what was studied, so study still matters. It works on learning that already happened.

misconceptions.name: Sleep is only a pause
misconceptions.correction: The brain can process recent learning during sleep.

misconceptions.name: Sleep teaches unseen material
misconceptions.correction: Sleep can help store what was learned, but it does not supply an unread lesson.

quest.title: Trace a lesson
quest.detail: In a made-up study day, mark learning first and later memory processing.

steps.title: Learn first, then it firms up

hook.stem: Rohan sleeps with his textbook under his pillow but never opens it. Will he remember the chapter?

options.feedback: Right. Memory first needs learning. Later steps can only firm up what was learned.
Sleep can firm up what you learned, but it cannot add a chapter you never read.

options.text: Only if he sleeps long enough.
options.feedback: No amount of sleep adds a chapter he never read. Learning comes first.

steps.teach: You learn first, and then the new memory gets firm. That later step is called consolidation.

parts: Divya reads her notes on the Mughals carefully,
and a week later the dates still come back easily.
example.spot: Divya reads her notes on the Mughals carefully,
example.feedback: Reading carefully is the learning step. Only after it can the memory firm up and last.

guided.stem: Faisal learns ten new Hindi words today. Over the next days the words feel steadier. What is that later step called?
guided.hint: It is the firming up after learning.

options.feedback: Yes. Consolidation is the firming up of a memory after learning.
Learning came first, today. The later firming up is consolidation.
The words are getting steadier, not fading. That is consolidation.

guided.stem: Mira skips her guitar lesson but sleeps well that night. Can sleep firm up the new chords for her?
guided.hint: What must happen before a memory can firm up?

options.text: No, she has not learned them yet.
options.feedback: Right. Sleep can only firm up what was learned.
Sleep does not supply a lesson. Learning comes first.
Extra sleep cannot add chords she never learned.

steps.takeaway: Learn first; the memory firms up later.

steps.title: Sleep helps memories last

hook.stem: Two groups learn word pairs. One sleeps, the other stays awake for the same hours. Which group recalls more later?

options.feedback: Right. In many studies, sleep after learning helps later recall.
Staying awake did not help more. In studies, sleep after learning helped recall.
In many studies, the sleep group recalled more.

steps.teach: Sleep after learning can help you recall more later. The sleeping brain helps firm up new memories.

example.ask: Tap what came between practice and morning.
parts: Gautam practises a new bowling action,
sleeps,
and the next morning his action feels smoother.
example.spot: sleeps,
example.feedback: Sleep after practice can help a new skill stick.

guided.stem: Sara learns a list of capitals at night, then sleeps. Ali learns it in the morning and stays awake all day. Who may recall more after the same gap?
guided.hint: Who slept after learning?

options.feedback: Yes. Sleep after learning can help later recall.
Ali stayed awake. In studies, sleep after learning tended to help recall more.
Both can recall some. Sleep after learning can help Sara recall more.

guided.stem: Tushar practises a tabla rhythm, then sleeps. The next day it comes more easily. What may have helped?
guided.hint: What happened between practice and the next day?

options.text: Sleep firmed up the new skill.
options.feedback: Right. Sleep after practice can help a new skill.
The tabla did not change. His memory of the rhythm did.
Studies find sleep after practice can help. It is not just luck.

steps.takeaway: Sleep after learning helps new memories stick.

steps.title: Quiet rest helps too

hook.stem: After a lesson, Jaya sits quietly for ten minutes with her eyes closed. Can that help her memory?

options.feedback: Right. Studies find short rest after learning can help new memories.
Sleep helps, but so can quiet rest while awake.

options.text: No, it is a waste of time.
options.feedback: Short quiet rest after learning can help new memories firm up.

steps.teach: Sleep is not the only help. A short spell of quiet rest after learning, awake and doing nothing, can also help new memories firm up.

parts: After learning the steps of a new dance,
Lakshmi sits quietly for a few minutes,
and later she recalls the steps well.
example.spot: Lakshmi sits quietly for a few minutes,
example.feedback: Quiet rest after learning can help new memories firm up.

guided.stem: After maths class, Ankit can scroll reels or sit quietly for five minutes. Which is more like the rest that helps memory?
guided.hint: Studies looked at rest with nothing to do.

options.feedback: Right. The rest in those studies was quiet, with nothing to do.
Reels keep the mind busy. The helpful rest in studies was quiet.

options.text: Starting a new lesson right away.
options.feedback: A new lesson keeps the mind busy. The helpful rest was quiet.

guided.stem: Between two exams, Rhea naps for a bit, then rests with her eyes closed. Which can help her new memories?
guided.hint: Can rest while awake help too?

options.text: Both the nap and the quiet rest.
options.feedback: Yes. Sleep can help, and quiet waking rest can help too.
The nap can help, and so can quiet waking rest.
Both can help new memories firm up.

steps.takeaway: Sleep helps memory, and so can quiet rest while awake.

concepts.title: Variable rewards
concepts.hook: A surprise good post can make the next swipe tempting, even after several dull ones.
concepts.rule: When rewards arrive at uneven times, the next try can seem worth checking. This can help explain repeated feed use.

claims.text: A reward now and then can draw more checks in some cases.
A study found that likes can shape posts. It did not test one set rule for each feed.
A variable reward comes after some tries but not others, so you cannot tell which try will bring it.

items.stem: In the hostel, Ali scrolls past dull posts, then finds a funny one. What makes him swipe again?

options.text: He cannot tell when the next good one comes.
options.feedback: A fun find now and then can make the next swipe feel worth it.

options.text: He knows the next one will be funny.
options.feedback: The last post was fun, so another feels likely. The next one can still be dull.

options.text: He knows every post will be dull.
options.feedback: If every post were sure to be dull, there would be little pull to swipe. Not knowing is the draw.

items.stem: Likes on Zoya's college post come in at random times. Why does she keep checking?

options.text: She cannot predict the next like.
options.feedback: Research found that social feedback can shape when people return to post or check.

options.text: Likes come on a fixed timer.
options.feedback: A steady clock would be easy to predict. Likes in the case arrive at uneven times.
A new check can feel due for a like. Likes can arrive at uneven times.

items.stem: In a feed with variable rewards, each swipe has a 1-in-5 chance of a fun clip. After five swipes, what is the chance of at least one?

options.feedback: The chance of no clip is 0.8 to the fifth power, about 33%. So at least one is about 67%, with no guarantee.

options.text: 100%, because one in five means a clip by swipe five.
options.feedback: One in five is a chance on each swipe, not a promise every fifth swipe. Five misses are still possible.
Each swipe has a 20% chance. Over five swipes, the chance of at least one good clip is about 67%.

items.stem: In a reward pattern, what does variable mean?

options.text: When the reward comes keeps changing.
options.feedback: The next payoff does not arrive after one fixed number of actions.
A good clip may follow a swipe. It does not follow each one.
Variable is about when the reward comes, not steady growth. The timing or count of payoffs can change.

items.stem: A friend says every feed works exactly like a slot machine. Why is that too strong?

options.feedback: The link is the unsure payoff. Feeds do not all have one set rule.

options.text: Every feed pays out on a fixed count.
options.feedback: A slot machine can suggest a strict rule. Feed posts and likes can vary in other ways.

options.text: All users get rewards at the same swipe.
options.feedback: The slot machine link invites one clock. Feeds and users can have different patterns.

items.stem: A reward comes after some checks but not others. That pattern is called ___.

options.feedback: Some actions bring a rewarding result while others do not.
Past checks can bring a reward, so a sure next one sounds fair. The gap can vary.
A reward on every fifth check is a set pattern. Here the reward comes after some checks, at no set gap.

items.stem: A classmate says people open feeds only for surprise rewards. What is missing?

options.feedback: People can also look for friends, news or a break.

options.text: Everyone opens feeds for one reason.
options.feedback: A shared app can make motives look alike. People may check news, friends, or other things.

options.text: Surprise rewards are the only reason.
options.feedback: A reward can pull another check. People also open feeds for news or friends.

items.stem: Why compare feeds to slot machines?

options.text: Not knowing when a win comes makes you try again.
options.feedback: The next nice post is hard to guess. That is the useful link.

options.text: Every swipe pays out on schedule.
options.feedback: A machine can pay on a fixed plan. This comparison is about not knowing when a good result will come.
The comparison is about the reward pattern, not who builds feeds. Not knowing when a win comes invites another try in both.

misconceptions.name: Every swipe rewards
misconceptions.correction: A good result can come after dull ones, with no set gap.

misconceptions.name: One cause explains all use
misconceptions.correction: People open feeds for many reasons, not just uncertain rewards.

Addictive Features of Social Media and Messenger Platforms

quest.title: Spot a pattern
quest.detail: Compare a made-up fixed reward sequence with an uneven one.

steps.title: Variable means you cannot tell when

hook.stem: A game gives a prize after some rounds but not others, with no pattern. How would you describe these prizes?

options.feedback: Right. When a reward comes at uneven, unknown times, it is called variable.
Not every round pays. Some do and some do not, with no pattern.
That would be a fixed pattern. Here the prize comes at uneven times.

steps.teach: A variable reward comes after some tries but not others. You cannot tell which try will bring it.

parts: Each time Zubin opens his messages,
there might be a reply or nothing at all.
example.spot: there might be a reply or nothing at all.
example.feedback: Sometimes a reply, sometimes nothing, with no way to tell. That is a variable reward.

guided.stem: A teacher gives a gold star after every third homework. Is that a variable reward?
guided.hint: Can you tell when the star comes?

options.feedback: Right. You know the star comes every third time, so it is fixed.
Here the star always comes every third time. That is fixed.

options.text: Yes, because it is a reward.
options.feedback: Any reward can be fixed or variable. This one comes on a set count.

guided.stem: At the village pond, some of Kavya’s casts catch a fish and most do not. What kind of reward pattern is this?
guided.hint: Does the catch come on a set count?

options.feedback: Yes. A catch comes after some casts but not others, with no set count.
A fixed pattern would pay on a set count. Fishing does not.
A fish is the reward. It just comes at uneven times.

steps.takeaway: Variable means the reward comes, but you cannot tell when.

steps.title: Not knowing keeps you checking

hook.stem: Why is it hard to stop pulling down to refresh a post for new likes?

options.text: The next refresh might bring one.
options.feedback: Right. When a like might come on the next try, the try seems worth it.

options.text: Each refresh always brings a like.
options.feedback: If it always did, there would be no surprise. The pull comes from not knowing.

options.text: The phone makes you do it.
options.feedback: The phone does not force it. Not knowing when a like comes pulls you back.

steps.teach: When a reward might come on the next try, that try seems worth making. So uneven rewards can keep people checking.

parts: Nikita finds a funny meme only now and then,
so she keeps swiping in case the next one is good.
example.spot: so she keeps swiping in case the next one is good.
example.feedback: Not knowing when the next good one comes keeps her swiping.

guided.stem: In a cricket card game, rare cards turn up in random packs. Omkar keeps opening packs. Why?
guided.hint: Can he tell which pack has a rare card?

options.text: The next pack might have one.
options.feedback: Yes. Not knowing which pack pays keeps him opening.

options.text: Every pack has a rare card.
options.feedback: Then they would not be rare. They come at random, which pulls him on.

options.text: He has to open them all.
options.feedback: Nothing makes him. The chance of a rare card pulls him on.

guided.stem: At a mela ring toss, some throws win a prize, with no pattern. Why do people keep trying for one more?
guided.hint: Can they tell which throw will win?

options.feedback: Right. When a win might come next, one more try feels worth it.
Then there would be no pull to try again. Wins come now and then.

options.text: The stall owner tells them to.
options.feedback: No one has to tell them. The chance that the next throw wins pulls them on.

steps.takeaway: Not knowing when a reward comes keeps us trying.

steps.title: One pull, not the whole story

hook.stem: Mansi opens a chat app many times a day. What could be the reason?

options.text: Many reasons, like friends, news or a break.
options.feedback: Right. Uneven rewards are one pull, but people open apps for many reasons.

options.text: Only the hope of a surprise reward.
options.feedback: That is one pull, but not the only one. Friends, news and breaks matter too.

options.text: Only because the app is new.
options.feedback: Being new is not the only reason. People open apps for many reasons.

steps.teach: Uneven rewards are one reason people keep checking feeds, not the only one. Feeds differ, and so do people.

parts: Kiran opens his feed after class
to see what his cousins posted from the wedding.
example.spot: to see what his cousins posted from the wedding.
example.feedback: His reason is family news, not a surprise reward. People open feeds for many reasons.

guided.stem: Tanmay keeps opening a cricket score app during a match. What is the most likely reason?
guided.hint: What does a score app give him?

options.feedback: Right. People also open apps for news, like a match score.

options.text: Only the hope of a surprise reward.
options.feedback: Rewards are one pull, but here the news of the score matters most.
No app forces him. He wants the news.

guided.stem: Two friends use the same feed. One checks it for jokes, the other to keep up with classmates. What does this show?
guided.hint: Do they have the same reason?

options.text: People use feeds for different reasons.
options.feedback: Yes. Uneven rewards are one pull among many reasons.

options.text: They both want surprise rewards only.
options.feedback: Their reasons differ. One wants jokes, one wants to keep up.

options.text: Feeds pull everyone the same way.
options.feedback: People differ, so the same feed can pull them in different ways.

steps.takeaway: Uneven rewards are one pull, not the whole story.

concepts.title: If-then plans
concepts.hook: A plan tied to a clear moment can help turn a goal into an action.
concepts.rule: An if-then plan names a cue and the action to take when it appears. This link can help people start.

claims.text: An if-then plan links a clear cue to a chosen act.
Studies find that such plans can help goal pursuit compared with a goal alone.
An if-then plan names a clear moment to act, which is easier to notice than a vague goal.

items.stem: Om, a hostel student, says: “If dinner ends, then I open my notes.” What helps him start?

options.feedback: The plan links a visible moment to the first action, making it easier to notice.
The cue is clear, so action may be more likely. A plan cannot make it certain.
Dinner may seem like just a goal. The word if makes its end the start cue.

items.stem: Before a college quiz, Mira says only, “I will revise more.” What does her plan lack?

options.feedback: The wish names a goal but no moment that starts a chosen action.
A bigger wish can feel more firm. It still gives no clear moment to act.
A deadline names an end, not the moment to start. An if-then plan links a cue to a chosen action.

items.stem: 94 studies tested if-then plans. Scientists score help on a scale where 0.2 is small, 0.5 medium and 0.8 large. What did plans score?

options.feedback: Across 94 tests, plans had a medium-to-large effect (d = 0.65). That is not the same as a 65% success rate.
The 0.65 figure uses spread in scores as its unit. It does not mean 65 percentage points.
A bare goal may not trigger action. Across these tests, specifying a cue and action had a positive average effect.

items.stem: Lia's plan: “If I sit at my desk, then I draw.” What tells her to start?

options.feedback: The desk moment is the cue linked in advance to the drawing action.
Drawing is the action to start when the desk cue appears. It is not the cue itself.
Waiting for a mood leaves the start open. Her plan names a cue: sitting down at the desk.

items.stem: Sam's plan: “If I am free, I will study.” Why might it not work?

options.text: Being free is hard to notice.
options.feedback: A cue that is hard to spot may not prompt the action at a clear moment.

options.text: A vague cue works as well as a clear one.
options.feedback: Both sound like plans. A clear event is easier to spot when it is time to act.

options.text: All if-then plans work the same.
options.feedback: Both plans use if and then. A vague cue can still be hard to spot.

items.stem: In “if this, then that,” the then part is the ___.

options.feedback: It names the action that was linked, ahead of time, to the chosen moment.
The cue comes first, so it is easy to name. The then part names what to do.
A plan may include a reward, but the then part names the action to take when the cue appears.

items.stem: A coach says an if-then plan guarantees you will act. What is too strong?

options.feedback: The plans can help on average. They do not make each act sure.

options.text: Writing it makes the cue impossible to miss.
options.feedback: A written cue is easier to recall. Busy days can still hide or change it.

options.text: A written plan controls the future.
options.feedback: Writing a plan can make it feel firm. A cue may still be missed or changed.

items.stem: How would you explain an if-then plan to a friend?

options.text: Pick a moment, and decide what you will do then.
options.feedback: The cue comes first. The action is ready to go when that moment arrives.
Both name a goal, so they sound alike. This plan also names a cue and an act.

options.text: It promises you will always do it.
options.feedback: A cue can be missed or changed, so it is no promise. It links a named moment with a chosen act.

misconceptions.name: A wish is a plan
misconceptions.correction: A broad goal leaves the moment of action unspecified.

misconceptions.name: A plan guarantees action
misconceptions.correction: Even a specific cue-action link can be missed or changed.

sources.publisher: Gollwitzer and Oettingen, University of Konstanz
