quest.title: Find the cue
quest.detail: Mark the if part and then part in a made-up study plan.

steps.title: Link a moment to an action

hook.stem: Three students plan to revise. Who has a clear moment to start?

options.text: Asha: “If I finish dinner, then I open my notes.”
options.feedback: Right. Her plan links a clear moment, dinner ending, to one action.

options.text: Bunty: “I will revise more this week.”
options.feedback: That is a goal, but it names no moment to start.
A hope names no moment or action. An if-then plan names both.

steps.teach: An if-then plan links a moment to an action: “If this happens, then I will do that.” The moment is the cue to start.

parts: Ananya decides that
when the school bell rings at 4,
she will walk to the library.
example.spot: when the school bell rings at 4,
example.feedback: The bell is the if part: the clear moment that starts the action.

guided.stem: Vikram’s plan: “If I get off the bus, then I call my grandmother.” What is the cue?
guided.hint: The cue is the if part.

options.feedback: Yes. Getting off the bus is the moment that starts the call.
That is the then part, the action.
The phone is not a moment. The cue is getting off the bus.

guided.stem: Tara’s plan: “If I tie my shoes after school, then I go for a run.” Which part is the action?
guided.hint: The action is the then part.

options.feedback: Right. The then part names the action.
That is the if part, the cue.
That is when the cue happens. The action is the run.

steps.takeaway: If this moment comes, then I do that action.

steps.title: Pick a moment you will notice

hook.stem: Which cue is easiest to notice: “when I feel like it,” “when I have time,” or “when the 7 o’clock news ends”?

options.feedback: Right. It is a clear moment you cannot miss.
That feeling may never come at a clear moment.
Free time is hard to spot, so it may not start the action.

steps.teach: A goal like “study more” names no moment to start. A clear cue, like “after dinner,” is easy to notice.

parts: Instead of planning to practise someday, Dhruv picks a moment:
when he gets home from school,
he plays the flute.
example.spot: when he gets home from school,
example.feedback: Getting home is a clear moment, so it is easy to notice.

guided.stem: Sonal says, “I will drink more water.” Which line turns it into an if-then plan?
guided.hint: Look for a clear moment and an action.

options.text: “If I sit down for lunch, then I drink a glass of water.”
options.feedback: Yes. It links a clear moment to one action.

options.text: “I really want to drink more water.”
options.feedback: That is still a wish, with no moment to start.
Trying hard names no moment. An if-then plan needs a cue.

guided.stem: Which if part is clearest for starting homework?
guided.hint: Which one can you notice at a set moment?

options.text: If I finish my evening chai.
options.feedback: Right. Finishing chai is a clear moment you will notice.

options.text: If I am in the mood.
options.feedback: A mood is hard to spot. It may not come at a clear moment.
Free time is hard to notice, so it may not start the action.

steps.takeaway: A clear moment is easy to notice; a vague one is easy to miss.

steps.title: It helps, but cannot promise

hook.stem: Studies compared people with only a goal to people who also made an if-then plan. What did they find?

options.feedback: Right. Across 94 tests, people with if-then plans did better on average.
They did make a difference. Across 94 tests, plans helped on average.

options.text: Everyone with a plan always acted.
options.feedback: Not always. Plans helped on average, but they cannot promise each act.

steps.teach: Across 94 tests, if-then plans helped people reach goals more than a goal alone. They help on average but cannot promise action.

visual.label: How much if-then plans helped, across 94 tests

example.ask: Tap where the plan did not work.
parts: Govind plans, “If I wake up, then I stretch,” and he stretches most days,
but not on the day he oversleeps.
example.spot: but not on the day he oversleeps.
example.feedback: The plan helps on most days, but it cannot promise every time.

guided.stem: Kriti made an if-then plan to read after dinner. One night a cousin visits and she skips it. What does this show?
guided.hint: Can a plan promise every act?

options.feedback: Yes. A plan helps on average, but things can still get in the way.
It helps on most nights. One skip does not make it useless.
Across 94 tests they helped on average. They just cannot promise each time.

guided.stem: Two cricket teams set a goal to practise catching. One team also adds if-then plans. Which team is likely to practise more?
guided.hint: What did studies find on average?

options.feedback: Right. On average, if-then plans helped people act on goals.

options.text: The team with only the goal.
options.feedback: Studies found the opposite, on average.
Across 94 tests, plans made a real difference on average.

steps.takeaway: If-then plans help on average, but they cannot promise action.

concepts.title: The spotlight effect
concepts.hook: A small slip can feel huge to us. Others may notice it less.
concepts.rule: The spotlight effect means we may guess too many people took note. Some still do.

claims.text: In a shirt test, wearers guessed too many people took note.
In a group talk, speakers thought their words stood out more than they did.

items.stem: Neha wears a bright shirt to college. She thinks the whole class will remember it. What is she overestimating?

options.feedback: In the test, the wearers guessed too high. Fewer people knew the shirt image.
A bright shirt catches her own eye. The effect asks how many others took note.
The price is not the point here. The effect is about how many people she expects noticed the shirt.

items.stem: Asha trips over one word in a cricket club talk. She thinks everyone remembers. What is going on?

options.text: It felt bigger to her than to them.
options.feedback: In a group talk, speakers guessed their words stood out more than they did.
The slip stands out to Asha. Other listeners may have paid it little mind.
It may not stand out to most people. Yet some listeners can still catch it.

items.stem: People wore an odd shirt and guessed 46% of others would notice it. About what percent really did?

options.feedback: Only about half as many people named the image as the wearers had guessed.
The 46% guess is easy to recall. Only about 23% of others named the image.
That is far above the result. About 23% named the image, half of what the wearers had guessed.

items.stem: What is the spotlight effect?

options.text: Thinking others notice us more than they do.
options.feedback: Our own experience is vivid, so it can loom larger than it does to observers.
The mistake feels vivid from the inside, but that feeling can overstate how much others noticed.
The name comes from stage lights, but the effect is about thinking others notice us more than they do.

items.stem: Why does a small mistake feel huge to the one who made it?

options.text: They lived every detail of it.
options.feedback: That vivid view from the inside can pull your guess about how much others saw.

options.text: A slip stands out the same to everyone.
options.feedback: The maker felt every detail. Others may have been busy with their own thoughts.

options.text: Others have the same inside view.
options.feedback: The slip filled the maker's mind. Others may have had many other things to watch.

items.stem: The spotlight effect is a bad guess about other people's ___.

options.feedback: The bias is in guessing how much others notice what we do or how we look.
The slip may feel big to her. This effect asks how many others took note.
The effect is not about how tall people are. It is about a guess of how much others pay attention.

items.stem: A friend says the spotlight effect means nobody notices mistakes. What is wrong?

options.feedback: Some observers may notice; the key is that the person often guesses too many.

options.text: The guess is always too high.
options.feedback: The group trend can sound like a fixed law. Any one guess may still be right.
People often notice less than we fear. Some can still spot the mistake.

items.stem: Which line fairly states the spotlight effect?

options.text: My moment feels bigger to me than to others.
options.feedback: The research concerns a gap between my guess and what observers recall.

options.text: Others think about me all day.
options.feedback: The moment looms large to us. Others may give it far less thought.
Some people do notice. The research finds that fewer notice than we guess, not that nobody does.

misconceptions.name: Everyone noticed
misconceptions.correction: Our own vivid view can make an event seem more visible to others than it was.

misconceptions.name: Nobody ever notices
misconceptions.correction: Some people may take note. The guess is often too high.

steps.title: Fewer people notice than we think

hook.stem: Sumit spills chai on his shirt before class. He thinks the whole class sees it. What is more likely?

options.text: Fewer people notice than he thinks.
options.feedback: Right. In a study, people guessed twice as many noticed their shirt as really did.
In studies, far fewer noticed than people guessed.
Some may notice, just fewer than he thinks.

steps.teach: We think more people notice us than really do: the spotlight effect. In one study, wearers of an odd shirt guessed 46% noticed; about 23% did.

visual.label: People who noticed an odd T-shirt

parts: Prerna gets a bad haircut and hides all day, yet
at lunch only one friend says anything.
example.spot: at lunch only one friend says anything.
example.feedback: Far fewer people noticed than she feared.

guided.stem: Raghav wears odd socks to a wedding and thinks all the guests saw. What is more likely?
guided.hint: Do people notice us as much as we think?

options.feedback: Yes. We tend to think more people notice us than really do.
Far fewer people notice than we tend to think.

options.text: The guests talk about it all night.
options.feedback: That is a big guess. Fewer people notice than we tend to think.

guided.stem: On a train, Ayesha’s phone rings loudly with a funny ringtone. She thinks the whole coach will remember. What is going on?
guided.hint: Compare her guess with what others notice.

options.text: She guesses more noticed than really did.
options.feedback: Right. That gap between her guess and what others notice is the spotlight effect.
Fewer people notice and recall than we tend to think.
Some may hear it. The point is she guesses too many will remember.

steps.takeaway: Fewer people notice us than we think.

steps.title: Our own view makes it loom large

hook.stem: Why does a small slip in a speech feel so big to the speaker?

options.text: They felt every second of it.
options.feedback: Right. The speaker’s own view is vivid, so the slip looms large.

options.text: The crowd talks about it for days.
options.feedback: Usually not. The slip feels bigger to the speaker than to the crowd.
Small slips are small. They just feel big from the inside.

steps.teach: We live every detail of our own slip, so it feels huge to us. We then guess others saw it just as clearly.

example.ask: Tap how big it felt to him.
parts: Arush says one wrong word in his group talk,
and he replays it all night,
though no one mentions it.
example.spot: and he replays it all night,
example.feedback: His own vivid view makes the slip loom larger for him than for the others.

guided.stem: In a debate, Simran pauses for a second and thinks everyone saw her freeze. Why does it feel so big to her?
guided.hint: Whose view is the most vivid?

options.text: She lived every detail of it.
